Start here

Your repeatable image-first algorithm
  1. Localize: focal vs diffuse; parenchyma vs vessel vs pleura vs airway.
  2. If nodule: solitary or multiple? Solitary → margin + calcification/fat. Multiple → distribution.
  3. Map multiple nodules to the secondary lobule: random, centrilobular, or perilymphatic.
  4. If airspace opacity: GGO vs consolidation, then ask what is replacing air: fluid, pus, blood, or cells.
  5. If diffuse lines: smooth septal thickening with preserved architecture vs distorted fibrotic architecture.
  6. Use the history last—but decisively: heart disease, hemoptysis, birds/exposure, chemotherapy, asbestos, systemic vasculitis.
Professor-level framing

Imaging narrows; context decides.

The lecture repeatedly emphasizes that several diseases can look similar on CT. Airspace opacity is not a diagnosis. Pneumonia, edema, hemorrhage, and tumor can all replace alveolar air and produce overlapping GGO/consolidation.

Core habit: describe the pattern first, then attach the clinical story.
Exam trap: jumping straight from “white lung” to pneumonia without asking whether the stem gives fever, heart disease, hemoptysis, chemotherapy, or another discriminator.

Exam sheet

Core map: abnormal image → localize → classify pattern → use secondary-lobule anatomy / morphology → attach clinical context → build differential. Describe before diagnosing.

Part I — Core framework & must-know content

Question to askWhat it tells youLecture-level move
Focal or diffuse?Sets the major branchFocal: nodule/opacity. Diffuse: edema, ILD/fibrosis, DAD, HP, sarcoid, hemorrhage/vasculitis.
Solitary or multiple nodules?Changes characterization strategySolitary → margin/calcification/fat. Multiple → distribution.
Where are multiple nodules relative to the secondary lobule?Routes to mechanismRandom → hematogenous; centrilobular → airway/inhaled; perilymphatic → lymphatics.
GGO or consolidation?Degree of airspace fillingSame etiologies can make both; history separates edema, pus, blood, cells.
Are lines smooth or is architecture distorted?Edema vs fibrosisSmooth septal thickening/effusions → edema. Distortion/traction/honeycomb → fibrosis.
Is the primary abnormality in vessel, pleura, or airway?Routes to PE, mesothelioma, bronchiectasisVessel filling defect; pleural nodularity/effusion; airway > artery.

Normal-to-abnormal bridge: secondary pulmonary lobule

Center: distal airway + pulmonary artery. This is why inhaled/small-airway processes create centrilobular nodules.
Periphery / septa: pulmonary veins + lymphatics; lymphatics also track pleura and bronchovascular bundles. This is why sarcoid becomes perilymphatic.

Solitary nodule logic

FindingMeaning in this lectureClosest mimic/trap
Spiculated + noncalcifiedHighly concerning for cancerDo not diagnose histology from spiculation alone.
Dense calcificationUsually benign; granuloma commonLecture simplifies calcification as reassuring; pattern still matters clinically.
Fat + smooth + popcorn calcificationHamartomaDo not call a partially calcified lesion malignant just because not every component is calcified.
Smooth endobronchial + marked enhancementCarcinoidSmooth does not mean “not a neoplasm.”

Primary lung-cancer CT patterns

CancerPatternExam discriminator
AdenocarcinomaMore peripheral; part-solid, ground-glass → solid; may appear as consolidationPeripheral part-solid lesion
Squamous cellMore central; cavitation commonCentral cavitary lesion
Small cellBulky mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy; paraneoplastic syndromes notedNodes dominate

Multiple nodules: distribution is diagnosis-generating

DistributionAnatomic logicLecture causesStem clue
RandomNo lobular relationship; hematogenous routeMetastases; infection such as miliary TBMany scattered nodules throughout lungs
CentrilobularAirway/pulmonary-artery centerHP; respiratory bronchiolitisBird/farm/etc exposure
PerilymphaticSepta, pleura, bronchovascular lymphaticsSarcoid; lymphangitic carcinomatosisHilar nodes + nodules along fissures/septa

Airspace opacity: same picture, different substance

Air replaced byProcessClinical clue
FluidPulmonary edemaHeart disease, septal thickening, effusions
PusPneumoniaFever/infectious context
BloodPulmonary hemorrhageHemoptysis, vasculitis/SLE, trauma, anticoagulation/inhalation injury
CellsTumorOncologic context / focal or persistent process
GGO vs consolidation: the lecture treats them as different densities/degrees of airspace filling. A process that can cause consolidation can also cause GGO.

Vascular, pleural, and airway must-knows

EntityMust recognizeHigh-value nuance
Acute PEPulmonary arterial filling defect ± infarctClinical likelihood matters because symptoms are nonspecific.
Chronic thromboembolic diseaseEccentric thread/web-like defectsConsider in unexplained dyspnea; CT helps assess potentially surgically treatable disease.
GPACavitary nodules; hemorrhage may cause GGO/consolidationLecture: nodules 90%, cavitation 50%, c-ANCA positive.
MesotheliomaNodular pleural thickening + effusionAsbestos association; pleural plaques are a separate asbestos-related finding.
BronchiectasisSignet-ring: airway > adjacent arteryCylindrical, varicoid, cystic; often linked to infection/aspiration.

Part II — Testable distinctions & application

Question-stem decoder

If the stem gives…First identify…Then check…Avoid…
Solitary lung noduleBenign vs malignant morphologySpiculation, calcification, fat, endobronchial location, enhancementAssuming “nodule = cancer”
Many tiny nodulesDistributionRandom vs centrilobular vs perilymphaticUsing total number of nodules as the main discriminator
Diffuse GGO/consolidationAirspace fillingHeart disease, fever, hemoptysis, injury/drugsCalling the CT itself diagnostic of pneumonia
Linear opacitiesInterstitial patternSmooth septa vs distorted architectureEquating all lines with fibrosis
Bird/farm/cheese/malt/hot-tub exposureHPCentrilobular GGO; acute vs chronic fibrotic changesChoosing sarcoid without a perilymphatic pattern
Asbestos + unilateral pleural abnormalityPleural diseaseNodular thickening/effusion vs calcified plaquesCalling plaques themselves mesothelioma
Hemoptysis + SLE/vasculitisPulmonary hemorrhageDiffuse GGO/consolidation; cavitary nodules if GPALetting a pneumonia-looking CT override the history
Contrast CT + acute chest pain/dyspneaPulmonary arterial problemIntraluminal filling defect ± infarctSearching first for airway disease

Fastest high-yield separations

Edema vs fibrosis:
Edema = smooth septal lines + effusions + cardiac context.
Fibrosis = irregular reticulation + traction/honeycomb + architectural distortion.
HP vs sarcoid:
HP = centrilobular / airway-centered + exposure.
Sarcoid = perilymphatic + hilar/mediastinal nodes.
Adeno vs squamous vs small cell:
Peripheral part-solid vs central cavitary vs bulky mediastinal nodes.
Bronchiectasis vs lung cysts:
Trace dilated tubes and compare airway with adjacent artery; airway > artery supports bronchiectasis.

Professor-emphasized caveats

  • Imaging often produces a differential, not certainty. Clinical history is essential for airspace opacity.
  • Calcified nodules are usually benign in the lecture framework, but the useful exam move is to recognize the specific benign patterns shown.
  • Multiple nodules require distribution analysis. “Multiple = metastatic” is an intentional oversimplification to avoid.
  • Fibrosis distorts. The professor explicitly contrasts clean, orderly septal lines with the pulled, curved, disorganized architecture of fibrosis.
  • DAD can progress to fibrosis. The lecture uses chemotherapy injury to make the temporal sequence memorable.
